title: Flip (2)

jokes.text: Larry insists Carol Burnett was the first person he called, then is immediately contradicted by Ellen DeGeneres walking out to confirm he called her on Tuesday
jokes.setup: Larry effusively tells Carol she was 'literally, honestly the first person I called' for his final show, building it up with repeated emphasis
jokes.punchline: Ellen DeGeneres walks out to a cheering audience and confirms Larry called her on Tuesday — before he called Carol on Wednesday
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed bit that uses Larry's defining character flaw — his pathological need to flatter while being fundamentally dishonest — as the engine. The physical payoff of Ellen literally walking out mid-lie is perfect structure: the setup is all earnestness, the punchline is irrefutable evidence. It works because it's rooted entirely in who Larry is. The joke lands hardest on rewatch because you see Larry digging deeper and deeper before the trap springs. Earns its high score because it's narratively clever, character-specific, and the comedic timing of the entrance is exquisite.

dialogue.line: Carol reveals she wasn't the first person Larry called, exposing his lie

jokes.text: Ellen: 'Um, Tuesday morning.' / Carol: 'You called me on Wednesday.'
jokes.setup: Ellen is asked simply when Larry called her
jokes.punchline: Her flat 'Tuesday morning' lands like a verdict, immediately followed by Carol's quiet, devastating 'You called me on Wednesday' — no anger, just the plain arithmetic of Larry's deception
jokes.explanation: The economy here is exceptional — two short lines deliver the entire comedic payload of the setup. The deadpan delivery (inferred from the show's no-laugh-track register) makes it land harder than any big reaction would. The audience laugh marker confirms the impact. Scores 8+ on craft because the joke is essentially pure structure and economy: maximum information, minimum words, perfectly placed.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Please, this is my last night.' [audience laughs as he tries to use sentimentality to escape accountability]
jokes.setup: Larry has been definitively caught calling Carol on Wednesday, not Tuesday
jokes.punchline: Rather than apologize or laugh it off, Larry invokes his last night as a shield — weaponizing pathos to dodge embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy. His instinct is never to own a mistake but to pivot to self-pity. The audience laugh confirms they've clocked it too. Works as a running gag seed — he'll deploy this manipulation repeatedly through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ellen
dialogue.line: Larry called me Tuesday morning

dialogue.speaker: Carol Burnett
dialogue.line: Wednesday

jokes.text: Larry: 'A lot of people don't know I started out as a plate spinner'
jokes.setup: Carol Burnett is praising Larry's versatility on his final show, saying she had 'no idea' he was so versatile
jokes.punchline: Larry, with total sincerity, claims to have started as a plate spinner — an absurd, anachronistic vaudeville skill — then adds 'people will catch up eventually'
jokes.explanation: A quietly absurd moment where Larry's narcissism and delusion collide. 'Plate spinner' is so specific and odd that it's funny on its own, but 'people will catch up eventually' — delivered with complete seriousness — elevates it. The joke is that Larry genuinely believes this about himself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Don't do this to me... this is my last night

jokes.text: Carol Burnett: 'I wish I still had my show so I could have you on' — on Larry's last night, repeatedly redirecting to herself
jokes.setup: Larry keeps trying to make the conversation about his last night; Carol keeps expressing how much she admires him
jokes.punchline: Carol's praise keeps accidentally centering herself ('I wish I still had my show') — which is the exact same self-absorption Larry is guilty of
jokes.explanation: A sustained ironic comedy of competing narcissisms — two entertainment legends both trying to be gracious while subtly making it about themselves. The rewatch bonus comes from recognizing the structural mirror: Carol is doing what Larry always does. Craft is solid but the payoffs are soft — it's a mood joke more than a punchline joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I wish I still had my show so I could have you on

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is my last night' [third time in the conversation, as Carol keeps talking about herself]
jokes.setup: Carol is excitedly describing how she does Q&As on tour now, while Larry is trying to get some last-night gravitas
jokes.punchline: Larry inserts 'this is my last night' again, now clearly a running gag — the phrase has become a comedic tic of desperate self-assertion
jokes.explanation: The running gag is well-established by now and each deployment earns incrementally bigger laughs. Not exceptional craft on its own, but effective as a callback and character beat — Larry's petulant need for the night to be about him is both funny and faintly tragic.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: going out like this as a liar

jokes.text: Carol: 'What a shame it would be that you would go out like this as a liar'
jokes.setup: Larry has been caught lying about calling Carol first; the segment is winding down with attempted warmth
jokes.punchline: Carol suddenly pivots from warm sentiment to drily calling Larry a liar — perfectly landing as she smiles and says 'but anyway...'
jokes.explanation: Carol threading the needle between warm tribute and sharp puncture. The phrase 'go out like this as a liar' is perfectly calibrated — devastating but delivered with a smile. The 'but anyway...' pivot makes it funnier by refusing to dwell. Good economy, strong callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Carol Burnett
dialogue.line: It's not written like some of this stuff

jokes.text: Larry: 'It's not written like some of this stuff' [audience laughs — the irony that his 'spontaneous' show is clearly scripted]
jokes.setup: Carol describes her unscripted Q&A touring shows as free-flowing and spontaneous
jokes.punchline: She contrasts it with 'some of this stuff' — gesturing at Larry's show — implying it's heavily scripted, which is funny given the show's meta-layer (we're watching a scripted show about a scripted show)
jokes.explanation: A gentle meta-joke that works on two levels: within the show, it's Carol poking at late-night artifice; for the HBO audience, there's a meta-layer about The Larry Sanders Show itself being scripted. Not a huge laugh moment but clever.

jokes.text: Larry's introduction of Sean Penn: 'We've dreamed of having him on. He's probably never dreamed of being here.'
jokes.setup: Standard gushing talk-show guest introduction
jokes.punchline: Larry mid-intro acknowledges the asymmetry — Larry fawns, Penn doesn't care — which is unusually self-aware for a host introduction
jokes.explanation: A quietly good self-aware line that punctures talk-show ritual. Larry essentially admits the guest is doing them a favor while they pretend it's mutual. Character-appropriate for Larry's blend of obsequiousness and occasional honesty.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Was the script that bad?

jokes.text: Sean Penn about his non-L.A. residency — Larry: 'Well, thank you for coming.' Penn: 'Sure. Let's not make a big deal about it.' Larry: 'It could be a long flight.'
jokes.setup: Larry confirms Penn doesn't live in L.A. and immediately treats it as a heroic sacrifice
jokes.punchline: Penn deflects the gratitude ('let's not make a big deal'), but Larry insists it IS a big deal — the comedy is Larry's compulsive need to over-thank guests versus Penn's celebrity indifference
jokes.explanation: A decent character beat — Larry's sycophancy vs. Penn's cool — but not especially original. The back-and-forth is functional rather than exceptional. Sets up the Penn segment's dynamic but isn't the funniest expression of it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Who's on the low end?

jokes.text: Sean Penn describes refusing to put away his script on the plane and the stewardess invoking FAR (Federal Aviation Regulations) — 'That you're not allowed to have a script?'
jokes.setup: Sean Penn is telling a story about a stewardess asking him to put away his reading material for landing
jokes.punchline: The absurdity that the FAA apparently has a regulation that could be construed as covering scripts — 'So marshals could come in here right now because I've violated a FAR'
jokes.explanation: The joke is character-specific to Sean Penn's famous combativeness and his self-important artist persona. The detail that he wasn't even reading the script — 'just trying to annoy her' — is the best line and reveals character. Good but not exceptional; the story meanders slightly before landing.

dialogue.speaker: Sean Penn
dialogue.line: He's the most insecure man I've ever met

jokes.text: Sean Penn: 'I just decided no.' [matter-of-fact, about refusing a stewardess on a plane]
jokes.setup: The stewardess tells Penn he has to put away his script for landing
jokes.punchline: 'I just decided no' — delivered with the complete calm of a man who has never once considered that rules might apply to him
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly skewer Sean Penn's celebrity entitlement. The economy is exceptional — 'I just decided no' contains an entire worldview. It works because it sounds exactly like something Sean Penn would say, delivered straight without self-awareness. The craft here is in how much character is compressed into a single short sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Sean Penn
dialogue.line: He's asking me, 'How was I?' before the director even says cut.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Was the script that bad?' [after Penn describes defying the stewardess over a script]
jokes.setup: Sean Penn has just described his principled stand against putting away his script on the plane, framed as a matter of artistic integrity
jokes.punchline: Larry punctures the whole self-important story with 'Was the script that bad?' — reframing Penn's stand as possibly just embarrassment about the material
jokes.explanation: A perfect talk-show host joke. Larry appears to be playing straight-man throughout the story, then lands this line that reframes everything. The implication — maybe Penn wanted to hide the script because it was terrible — is a sharp Hollywood insider burn. Economy is near-perfect. Penn's laugh confirms it landed. One of the episode's best quick jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Sean Penn
dialogue.line: But he was constantly after her, trying to get in her trailer.

jokes.text: Penn on defying the stewardess: 'I was just wanting — trying to annoy her. Just trying to annoy the stewardess.' [applause]
jokes.setup: Larry asks why Penn needed to keep the script during landing — implying artistic necessity
jokes.punchline: Penn reveals he wasn't even reading it — he just wanted to annoy the stewardess. The principled stand was purely petulant
jokes.explanation: The best moment of the Penn segment. The entire story has been framed as a First Amendment/artist's rights issue — Penn resisting petty authority. Then he deflates his own mythology completely: 'just trying to annoy her.' It's the funniest possible reframing of celebrity entitlement as simple, childish spite. The audience applauds because it's unexpectedly honest. Strong structure, exceptional character integration — this captures Sean Penn's persona perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Allen
dialogue.line: Hey, close the fucking door!

jokes.text: Penn mentions the Hurlyburly cast: 'Kevin Spacey, Anna Paquin, my wife Robin, Garry Shandling...' — Larry: 'What a fantastic cast, huh?'
jokes.setup: Sean Penn lists the impressive cast of Hurlyburly
jokes.punchline: Garry Shandling is listed among genuine movie stars (Spacey, Paquin, Penn's wife Robin Wright), and Larry/Garry immediately says 'What a fantastic cast, huh?' — shameless self-congratulation that Penn then dryly agrees with
jokes.explanation: A glorious meta-moment: Garry Shandling (playing Larry Sanders, who is loosely Garry Shandling) is in a real movie with Sean Penn, and the joke layers the real and fictional. Larry calling himself a 'fantastic cast' via the 'what a fantastic cast, huh?' line is both Larry's narcissism AND Shandling winking at the audience. Rewatch bonus because you catch more layers each time.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Allen
dialogue.line: I took a shit this morning with more talent

jokes.text: Larry: 'Who's on the low end of the ability there?' Penn: 'I'm not gonna go there... but we made a great movie.'
jokes.setup: Larry notes that the Hurlyburly cast represents 'the spectrum of acting ability' — clearly setting up Penn to slag someone
jokes.punchline: Penn demurs with 'I'm not gonna go there' — but the pause before 'but we made a great movie' implies he absolutely would, and the audience fills in the blank (Shandling)
jokes.explanation: The joke works on implication rather than statement — both more elegant and funnier. Penn's restraint is the punchline, because the audience knows exactly who the low end is. The unsaid is funnier than anything Penn could say aloud.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Allen
dialogue.line: Fucking celebrity circle jerk

jokes.text: Backstage: Penn tells a producer that Shandling is 'the most insecure man I've ever met in my life' — 'Before our director would even say cut, he'd look at me and say, How was I? Relentless.'
jokes.setup: Penn is backstage after the on-air segment; a producer compliments the segment
jokes.punchline: Penn delivers a devastating character takedown of Shandling: before the director even called cut, Shandling was asking for validation — 'Relentless'
jokes.explanation: This is Garry Shandling writing a vicious, deeply self-aware joke about his own insecurity. Penn is describing Larry Sanders but also Garry Shandling — the meta-collapse is thrilling. 'Before the director even says cut' is perfectly specific. 'Relentless' as the button is great economy. Character integration is exceptional because only this show, with this level of self-examination, could make this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Allen
dialogue.line: Jungle 2 Jungle? Underrated.

jokes.text: Penn: 'I don't know if he knew that my wife and I were together, but he was constantly after her, trying to get in her trailer.'
jokes.setup: Penn is already on a roll describing Shandling's neediness; the story escalates
jokes.punchline: Penn casually drops that Shandling was apparently pursuing his wife Robin Wright — 'trying to get in her trailer' — said with the same deadpan matter-of-factness as the previous anecdote
jokes.explanation: A dark escalation joke — the 'constant insecurity' story pivots into something more scandalous. The straight-faced delivery ('I don't know if he knew we were together') implies Sean Penn might have underreacted, which is its own joke. Deeply character-specific to the Shandling self-flagellation that runs through the show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, my god. Jerry Seinfeld!

jokes.text: Tim Allen bursts in backstage: 'Hey, close the fucking door!' — immediately launching into Hollywood agent gossip about Jon Stewart
jokes.setup: We cut to a backstage scene; Tim Allen enters
jokes.punchline: His opening line is an aggressive command rather than a greeting — establishing his character as a blunt, profane Hollywood survivor before any context is given
jokes.explanation: Decent character establishment — the unexpectedness of Tim Allen being the agent-world cynic is funny casting. But the joke is fairly broad and relies on the surprise of profanity rather than wit.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Seinfeld
dialogue.line: This show isn't going to be syndicated. Oh, that's right. That's me.

jokes.text: Agent about Jon Stewart leaving: 'He says he caught me in a lie. Right. Oh, my god, I told a fuckin' lie. I told him his fuckin' show would run for 20 years. He didn't seem to mind that lie.'
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart has left the agency because he caught the agent in a lie
jokes.punchline: The agent's contempt is that he told Stewart his show would run 20 years — an obvious, flattering lie — and Stewart was fine with that one. The lie he objected to was apparently something less comfortable
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood satire — the joke is that everyone in the industry operates on comfortable lies, and clients only object when the lie is uncomfortable. The 'he didn't seem to mind that lie' turn is excellent. Cynical but earned, a microcosm of the entire show's worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Seinfeld
dialogue.line: Then you're definitely doing the right thing

jokes.text: Agent: 'He's got nothing. I'm telling you, I took a shit this morning with more talent.'
jokes.setup: Agent is venting about Jon Stewart (in 1998, before Stewart took over The Daily Show)
jokes.punchline: The scatological hyperbole — 'I took a shit this morning with more talent' — lands as both gross and a funny period joke (this would age spectacularly given Stewart's later career)
jokes.explanation: The rewatch bonus is enormous — this line about Jon Stewart having no talent aged into one of the great unintentional irony jokes in TV history, given Stewart's subsequent cultural dominance. In 1998, it's a solid gross hyperbole; in retrospect, it's a masterclass in dramatic irony. Scored at face value for when it aired.

dialogue.speaker: Clint Black
dialogue.line: They said if I did real well, you'd have me back again

jokes.text: Agent and producer share a joint backstage — 'Where'd you get it?' 'Jimmy Federson. He gave it to me at the Simon Wiesenthal dinner.'
jokes.setup: Two TV industry figures share marijuana backstage
jokes.punchline: The joint came from the Simon Wiesenthal Center dinner — the most solemn, Holocaust-remembrance context imaginable as the source of weed
jokes.explanation: A genuinely original and audacious joke. The Simon Wiesenthal Center dinner is such a specific and incongruous source for marijuana that it's both brilliantly funny and slightly transgressive. The economy is perfect — just naming the event is enough. This is the kind of insider Hollywood joke that only The Larry Sanders Show could tell, and it justifies the 8+ score. The specificity ('Jimmy Federson' as a named dealer) adds another layer of deadpan absurdity.

jokes.text: Agent: 'I can't tell you how easy our job would be if we didn't have to deal with talent. But none of us are happy.'
jokes.setup: The agents are venting about difficult clients
jokes.punchline: 'But none of us are happy' — the pivot from complaining about talent to acknowledging universal misery, delivered as a resigned acceptance rather than a complaint
jokes.explanation: A solid industry-insider laugh — the nihilism of Hollywood agents summed up in one sentence. Functional but not exceptional. The joke is mostly in the delivery context rather than the words themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Play the damn song

jokes.text: Producer to Tim Allen on-air: 'Everybody in the business is gonna miss you so much.' Agent, under his breath immediately after: 'Fucking celebrity circle jerk.'
jokes.setup: On-camera Larry and Tim Allen are exchanging warm farewell sentiments
jokes.punchline: Cut to backstage — or said privately — agent mutters 'Fucking celebrity circle jerk,' completely deflating the on-air sincerity
jokes.explanation: The entire Larry Sanders Show thesis in three words. The joke works because the show earns its cynicism — we've just watched a genuinely emotional tribute segment, and this line is the necessary antidote. 'Celebrity circle jerk' is highly quotable and precisely captures the show's worldview. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Got another job.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, great.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Tell me.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It sucks.

jokes.text: Larry to Tim Allen as he's leaving: 'Jungle 2 Jungle? Underrated.'
jokes.setup: Tim Allen is rushing out; Larry is calling after him with a final compliment
jokes.punchline: The most sincere thing Larry can find to say about Tim Allen's career is that 'Jungle 2 Jungle' — a critically panned Tim Allen film — is 'underrated'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The economy is extraordinary — just four words convey Larry's desperate need to connect with every guest, his fundamental shallowness (THIS is his Tim Allen compliment?), and a perfect industry-insider joke about the film's quality. 'Underrated' applied to Jungle 2 Jungle is so wrong that it's devastating. It's also pure Larry Sanders: he's not being sarcastic, he genuinely seems to mean it, which makes it funnier. Highly quotable and earns the 8+ with its economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: asking 'fucking eggheads' about the Monroe Doctrine

jokes.text: Running gag: 'No flipping. We'll be right back.' — repeated after every commercial break throughout the episode
jokes.setup: Standard commercial break sign-off
jokes.punchline: On the final night of the show, 'no flipping' is both Larry's usual catchphrase and an increasingly poignant plea not to abandon him — building toward the 'you may now flip' payoff
jokes.explanation: Scored as the running gag aggregate — each individual instance contributes to the payoff of joke #35. The cumulative effect of 'no flipping' across the episode earns its place as a structural comedy device. The phrase becomes funnier and sadder with each repetition as the finale approaches.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: considering Hank's $300/week job with no benefits

jokes.text: Hank begins his heartfelt thank-you speech — Larry interrupts: 'Oh, my god. Jerry Seinfeld!'
jokes.setup: Hank has been waiting the entire episode for his moment to deliver a sincere thank-you speech; he finally gets the floor and begins
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately cuts him off to introduce Jerry Seinfeld — the most dismissive possible treatment of Hank's big moment, and completely in character
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. Hank's entire arc in this episode has been building to this speech, and it gets cut off by the exact thing that defines his relationship with Larry — being dismissed the moment someone more important arrives. The joke earns every point because it requires knowing Hank's character and his place in the hierarchy. The timing — Larry's sudden explosion of enthusiasm for Seinfeld mid-Hank-speech — is perfect. This is character comedy at the highest level.

jokes.text: Jerry Seinfeld to Larry: 'I think you're really doing the right thing.' — Larry: 'Thank you. That means so much to me.' — Seinfeld: 'And that was very touching, by the way, what you were saying.' Larry: 'Thank you. That was just the first part. I wasn't finished.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld is complimenting what he just heard — which was actually Hank's speech, not Larry's
jokes.punchline: Hank interjects that it was 'just the first part' — Seinfeld was moved by Hank, but everyone (including Seinfeld) assumes it was Larry's speech
jokes.explanation: A nice layered joke: Seinfeld's compliment goes to the wrong person (Larry accepts it), and Hank's correction — 'that was just the first part, I wasn't finished' — is both funny and sad. The joke compounds Hank's humiliation while Larry basks in unearned praise. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Bruno
dialogue.line: A man singing to a man. How fuckin' sick is that?

jokes.text: Seinfeld: 'We're certainly going to enjoy watching you in syndication after this.' Larry: 'This show isn't going to be syndicated.' Seinfeld: 'Oh, that's right. That's me. That is you. You're thinking of you.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld is offering a warm sentiment about Larry's legacy
jokes.punchline: He accidentally references his own Seinfeld syndication deal — one of the most lucrative in TV history — rather than Larry's show, which is ending without syndication. Larry corrects him and Seinfeld confirms 'you're thinking of you' with cheerful self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A genuinely exceptional joke that requires the real-world knowledge that Seinfeld was at this exact moment the most syndicating show in TV history, and The Larry Sanders Show was an acclaimed HBO series that would never see that money. The contrast is devastatingly specific. Seinfeld's cheerful 'that is you, you're thinking of you' is a perfect button — he's not mean, just obliviously rich. This is insider comedy at its finest and earns the 8+ score comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Bruno
dialogue.line: A man singing to a man. How fuckin' sick is that?

jokes.text: After Hank continues his speech: 'Every night?' Seinfeld asks; Hank confirms 'Every night.' Seinfeld: 'Then you're definitely doing the right thing.'
jokes.setup: Hank is delivering his speech about what a gift Larry's show has been to him, describing how every night was a gift
jokes.punchline: Seinfeld's 'then you're definitely doing the right thing' reframes Hank's tribute as evidence that the show should end — implying that if Hank benefited that much, it's been going on too long
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical reversal — Seinfeld takes Hank's sincere tribute and uses it as evidence that cancellation is correct. The joke also contains a subtle dig at Hank (if Hank thrived off this, maybe it wasn't high culture). The deadpan delivery and economy earn it. Strong structure: question, confirmation, pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Bruno
dialogue.line: There is no 'another time.' The party is over. This is it.

jokes.text: Clint Black: 'They said if I did real well, you'd have me back again.' [pause] 'Well, let's see how it goes.'
jokes.setup: Clint Black is thanking the audience for participating in 'this evening' — Larry's finale
jokes.punchline: He's been told he'd get to come back if he does well — on the final episode of a show that is ending. The deadpan 'well, let's see how it goes' suggests either he doesn't know the show is ending or he's playing along
jokes.explanation: A gentle absurdist joke playing on the futility of performing for 'next time' on a show's last episode. Slightly underplayed but that's appropriate for the tone. The humor is in the impossibility of what he's been promised.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Larry's joke about ending up with 'The Ropers' 9 times out of 10

jokes.text: Clint Black: 'I had a surprise for you.' Larry: 'What would that be?' Clint: 'It was a surprise for me — they forgot to tell me what it was.'
jokes.setup: Clint Black sets up a dramatic announcement about a surprise for Larry
jokes.punchline: The surprise was also a surprise to Black — he wasn't informed of his own bit
jokes.explanation: A neatly structured bit that plays on the chaos of live TV production — even the performers don't know what's happening. The 'so it's a surprise for everybody / for both of us' exchange is a clean double.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I can't get off the stool

jokes.text: Clint Black begins an elaborate emotional speech about what he's going to sing — Larry: 'Play the damn song.'
jokes.setup: Clint Black has been winding up for an extended speech about finding the right song that 'embodies what we all feel,' including a mention of Larry's shrink
jokes.punchline: Larry, who has been patiently watching this balloon expand, just says 'Play the damn song' — cutting through all the ceremony
jokes.explanation: Four words that deflate an entire comedic build. Pure Larry — impatient, uncomfortable with sentimentality, cutting through the very ceremony he ostensibly wants. The joke works because we've watched Larry demand sentimentality all episode, and now that he's getting it, he can't stand it. Good character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I hope we beat Leno

jokes.text: Beverly's new job: 'I'm gonna be the contestant coordinator for Jeopardy.' — 'I get to spend all day asking a bunch of fucking eggheads if they know anything about the Monroe Doctrine.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has a new job after the show ends
jokes.punchline: The Jeopardy job is described with complete contempt — 'bunch of fucking eggheads' — by someone who presumably has to pretend to be enthusiastic about them
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between what Jeopardy represents (intelligence, culture) and Beverly's complete disdain for it. 'Monroe Doctrine' as the example question is perfectly specific. Solid industry-adjacent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you had done it that way, we'd probably still be on the air

jokes.text: Beverly: 'Hank offered me a job. $300 a week with no benefits.' Pause. 'I'm sorry.' 'I'm thinking of taking it.'
jokes.setup: Beverly describes Hank's job offer as a genuine alternative to Jeopardy
jokes.punchline: The offer is so insulting ($300/week with no benefits) that it warrants an apology — but Beverly is still considering it, which makes both the offer and Beverly's situation funnier and sadder
jokes.explanation: A great Hank joke delivered in absentia — the $300/no benefits offer is so Hank that it doesn't even need setup. The 'I'm sorry' pause is excellent structure. The final 'I'm thinking of taking it' reveals Beverly's situation and Hank's power in one efficient beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And the part about whining about my ass. You're gonna miss that a little bit, aren't you?

jokes.text: Artie bumps a guest ('Bruno') from the show mid-song: 'The man is singing a fucking good-bye song.' — Bruno protests about next time — Artie: 'There IS no next time. The party is over. This is it.'
jokes.setup: A guest is being bumped from the final show as Clint Black sings; Artie is enforcing it with his usual brutality
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'there is no next time' has both practical truth (the show is ending) and existential weight — it doubles as a comment on mortality and television's transience
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie — ruthless, clear-eyed, no sentimentality about the mechanics. The comedy is in his complete absence of consolation: 'there is no next time, the party is over.' Rip Torn's delivery is the joke as much as the words. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Hank's explosive rant about being treated like 'the little fucking dog at the end of the couch'

jokes.text: Artie watches Clint Black sing a goodbye song to Larry: 'A man singing to a man. How fuckin' sick is that?' [then immediately sobs]
jokes.setup: Artie has been professionally brutal throughout; now Clint Black is singing and the emotion is hitting the room
jokes.punchline: Artie's response to being moved is to first express homophobic deflection ('how fuckin' sick is that?') and then immediately break down sobbing — the deflection making the emotion funnier
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Artie's character has been all edges and profanity — the idea that he's crying at a country singer serenading his host is the perfect character reversal. The homophobic deflection ('how fuckin' sick is that?') is both funny and revealing: Artie has to protect himself from the emotion by attacking it first. Then he immediately cries anyway. The beat is structured as: defensive joke → immediate contradiction by his own body. This is exceptional character comedy — only Artie, only this show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Thank you for not letting me say my thank you. I mean, I knew you guys were pieces of shit, but I, you know, I had no idea.

jokes.text: Artie standing alone, sobbing — then catching himself and covering with a cough
jokes.setup: Artie, the show's no-nonsense veteran producer, has just delivered his 'party is over' speech
jokes.punchline: He stands alone and silently weeps — then converts it to a cough when he realizes someone might see him — the toughest man on the show caught in a moment of genuine feeling
jokes.explanation: A perfect visual/reaction comedy beat that's also deeply moving. Rip Torn's Artie is the most emotionally defended character in the show — and seeing him break and then immediately cover the break is both hilarious and heartbreaking. The 'cough' conversion is the joke: he won't let the moment be real. This is the show at its highest level — comedy that doesn't sacrifice character. Justifies 8+ because it requires zero words to be devastating and funny simultaneously, and because it's entirely specific to Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Well, more money than pussy

jokes.text: Larry's closing speech: '9 times out of 10 you end up with the Ropers' — as his example of TV mediocrity
jokes.setup: Larry is giving his final speech about the risks of television and trying to do something fresh
jokes.punchline: 'The Ropers' — a real spinoff of Three's Company from 1979 — is Larry's shorthand for forgettable, mediocre TV, delivered mid-sincere speech as if everyone knows what he means
jokes.explanation: A nicely specific industry-insider joke in the middle of a sincere speech. 'The Ropers' is funnier than a generic placeholder would be — it's a real, specifically mediocre piece of television history. The joke works because Larry deploys it mid-sentiment without breaking stride.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: One more remark, and I swear, I'll fucking choke you with my hands!

jokes.text: Larry's final sign-off: 'You may now flip.' — a callback to 'No flipping' throughout the show
jokes.setup: Throughout the entire episode, Larry has been closing every commercial break with 'No flipping' — a running gag about not changing the channel
jokes.punchline: His final words are 'you may now flip' — releasing the audience with permission to do what he's been forbidding all night. It's sad, funny, and perfectly structured as an episode-length callback
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and earns every point of its score. It's been built across the entire episode — six iterations of 'no flipping' — and the inversion 'you may now flip' is both the comedic payoff and the emotional gut-punch of the series finale. It's funny and heartbreaking simultaneously. The structure is perfect: the punchline is the setup, and the setup is twenty-two minutes of television. Economy: three words. Character integration: completely Larry Sanders. Earned vs. cheap: the most earned laugh possible. This is what great sitcom writing looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And you, sir, are not in it, and you, sir, are not in it.

jokes.text: Larry collapses after the show — 'I can't get off the stool. I can't move my legs.' — 'Larry sprained his ankle. I should have waited another 6 months.'
jokes.setup: The show has just ended on an emotional high; Larry is basking in the applause
jokes.punchline: He physically cannot get off the stool — the emotional climax is immediately undercut by his ankle giving out. Artie's response is 'I should have waited another 6 months' — implying the show should have kept going (and could have, physically, since Larry is now incapacitated anyway)
jokes.explanation: Perfect deflation of a potentially overwrought finale moment. Larry can't even exit gracefully — his body betrays him. Artie's line ('I should have waited 6 months') is the real joke: it reframes the entire retirement decision as premature and arbitrary at the exact moment of its execution. Funny and a little cruel, which is the show's sweet spot.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's just a consulting gig, you know. That doesn't count.

jokes.text: Larry, being helped off the set: 'I hope we beat Leno.'
jokes.setup: Larry is in pain, being helped off the stage, having just ended his ten-year run with an emotional finale
jokes.punchline: His first concern after a decade-ending moment of profound personal significance is his ratings versus Jay Leno — even in physical distress, Larry's insecurity about competition never stops
jokes.explanation: This might be the single most character-specific joke in the episode. Larry has just delivered a genuinely moving farewell. He's being physically supported as he leaves. And his first thought is beating Leno. The joke requires the entire series of Larry Sanders to have built Larry's pathological competitiveness, and this line is the perfect summary of who he is. 'I hope we beat Leno' — five words that contain ten years of character work. Maximum character integration, maximum economy. Just barely edges below the 'you may now flip' callback because that one is structural perfection. But this might be funnier in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Rosie wants to come back nice this time, so she wants to have me come around one day a week to scare the shit out of her staff.

jokes.text: Artie enters the empty studio: 'Hello, stranger.' Hank: 'What are you doing here?' Artie: 'Oh, just being a sad and pathetic shithead like you.'
jokes.setup: Artie finds Hank alone in the empty studio after everyone has left
jokes.punchline: Artie's explanation for why he's there is the perfectly self-aware 'sad and pathetic shithead like you' — he owns his sentimentality by insulting both himself and Hank simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie — the warmest thing he can say is an insult. 'Sad and pathetic shithead like you' is Artie's love language and it perfectly encapsulates the show's approach to male emotional expression: affection through abuse. The self-inclusion ('like you') is the key — he's not superior, he's in the same boat. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Artie and Hank looking at Larry's desk: 'I don't know why we didn't try it before.' Artie: 'If you had done it that way, we'd probably still be on the air.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Hank are sitting in the empty set, looking at the desk from a different angle or arrangement
jokes.punchline: Artie suggests that one small staging change would have kept the show running — absurdly attributing ten years of creative struggle to something as simple as desk placement
jokes.explanation: A gentle absurdist joke that captures TV industry magical thinking — that everything could have been solved with one different production decision. Artie's deadpan delivery sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I'm such a prick

jokes.text: Artie's farewell speech to Larry: 'Your constant whining about the size of your ass, and all the shit you made me clean up because you were too much of a pussy to do it yourself... you made me laugh, and that's what I'm gonna miss.'
jokes.setup: Artie is attempting a heartfelt farewell to Larry — 'I'm not gonna get all gooey, kiddo'
jokes.punchline: The itemized list of Larry's flaws (ass whining, cowardice, making Artie do his dirty work) delivered as the preamble to a genuine expression of love — 'you made me laugh'
jokes.explanation: The emotional climax of Artie's character work, delivered as comedy. The joke structure is: Artie builds a catalog of Larry's failings with increasing specificity ('whining about the size of your ass' is particularly good), then pivots to genuine emotion. It works because we know Artie well enough to know this IS his version of 'I love you.' The 'ass whining' detail earns its place because it's absurdly specific. Strong structure, exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The part about whining about my ass — you're gonna miss that a little bit, aren't you? Because who else is gonna whine about their ass as much as me?'
jokes.setup: Artie has just mentioned 'your constant whining about the size of your ass' as one of Larry's defining traits
jokes.punchline: Rather than the straight-man embarrassment you'd expect, Larry leans into it — genuinely arguing that his ass-whining is a unique gift, something Artie will miss
jokes.explanation: Larry's narcissism applied to his own neuroses — he hears 'you whine about your ass' and thinks 'yes, and won't you miss that uniquely?' It's a perfect Larry move: converting a criticism into a boast. 'Who else is gonna whine about their ass as much as me?' has genuine quotability and reveals character economically.

jokes.text: Hank's final explosion: 'I spent the last 10 years being the butt of your jokes. The little fucking dog at the end of the couch!'
jokes.setup: Hank has been building resentment throughout the episode (interrupted speech, constant dismissals); now he explodes
jokes.punchline: The image Hank uses — 'the little fucking dog at the end of the couch' — is so specific, so self-aware, and so perfectly captures his role in the show's hierarchy that it functions as both comedy and pathos
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most emotionally complex joke and one of the series' great lines. 'The little fucking dog at the end of the couch' is a phrase that could only come from Hank Kingsley — it's both his self-pity and his self-awareness, his resentment and his acknowledgment of his own diminishment. It's funny because it's perfectly, absurdly specific; it's devastating because it's true. Jeffrey Tambor has built to this moment across six seasons. The originality is exceptional — this specific image, for this specific character, for this specific moment. It will be quoted for decades.

jokes.text: Hank's explosion: 'I spent the last 10 years being the butt of your jokes. The little fucking dog at the end of the couch!'
jokes.setup: Hank has finally snapped; he's delivering a genuine grievance about his treatment over 10 years
jokes.punchline: 'The little fucking dog at the end of the couch' — the image is both vivid and pathetic; it's Hank's self-conception that makes it funny while also being devastating
jokes.explanation: One of the series' great Hank moments. 'The little fucking dog at the end of the couch' is an image that perfectly captures his role and his awareness of it — it's absurd, specific, and devastating. The line is entirely Hank's: his grandiosity and his genuine pain are inseparable. The vulgarity ('fucking dog') attached to the pitiful image ('little dog at the end of the couch') creates perfect tonal dissonance. Justifies 8+ because the metaphor is original, deeply character-specific, and has genuine emotional weight beneath the comedy.

jokes.text: Hank: '...because this face was being seen by millions of people every night and there was lots of money and there was lots of pussy! Well, more money than pussy.'
jokes.setup: Hank is mid-explosion, justifying why he smiled and let himself be humiliated for ten years
jokes.punchline: He lists fame, money, and sexual access as his motivations — then immediately self-corrects: 'well, more money than pussy' — the self-correction landing harder than the original claim
jokes.explanation: The self-correction is everything. Hank sets up 'lots of money and lots of pussy' as his proud motivation — a cliché of Hollywood braggadocio — but the 'well, more money than pussy' undermines his own boast mid-sentence. It reveals Hank more completely in six words than most speeches could in a paragraph: he got the money, but not the validation he really wanted. Enormously quotable. Pure Hank. One of the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: Hank threatening Larry: 'One more remark, and I swear I'll fucking choke you with my hands!' — Larry: 'What's wrong with you?'
jokes.setup: Hank's explosion is reaching peak intensity
jokes.punchline: 'I'll fucking choke you with my hands' — the specificity of 'with my hands' is absurdly redundant (how else would one choke someone?) and deflates the threat comically. Larry's flat 'what's wrong with you?' is the perfect straight-man button
jokes.explanation: The 'with my hands' addition to a choking threat is a quietly funny bit of bad-at-threatening energy. The comedy is in the redundancy — Hank is so worked up he's lost the ability to make a credible threat. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Hank: 'There is a book called Hank Kingsley, but there's a new chapter, and you sir are not in it. And you sir are not in it.'
jokes.setup: Hank is attempting a dramatic final declaration of independence
jokes.punchline: The metaphor of 'a book called Hank Kingsley' is both grandiose and absurdly self-important; saying 'you are not in it' twice (to both Larry and Artie) is pompous escalation; the whole image is bathos — Hank as the hero of his own mediocre novel
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Hank imagining himself as the protagonist of a significant life narrative — 'a book called Hank Kingsley' — when the whole episode has confirmed his supporting-character status. The repetition of 'you sir are not in it' adds pomposity. It's funny because it's the most Hank thing possible: grandiose, slightly misworded, and deeply earnest.

jokes.text: After Hank storms off: Larry: 'He's such a goddamn idiot, but I sure do love him.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just delivered an epic, profanity-laced, emotionally genuine farewell rant
jokes.punchline: Larry's response is the most reductive possible: 'goddamn idiot' as his primary assessment, with 'but I sure do love him' as an afterthought — the order matters entirely
jokes.explanation: Larry watching someone pour their heart out and summarizing it as 'goddamn idiot' first is perfect characterization. The 'but I sure do love him' saves it from being cruel, but the order — idiot first, love second — tells you everything about Larry as a person. Clean economy.

jokes.text: Artie announces retirement: 'I'm just sick and tired of all the bullshit, scraping and bowing to fucking executives who think that creativity is nothing but an accounting problem.' Then: 'I thought you took the job on Roseanne.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers a passionate speech about retiring from television, fed up with executives and bullshit
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately deflates the whole thing: 'I thought you took the job on Roseanne.' Artie's permanent retirement has already been compromised before it's even official
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured deflation. Artie builds a righteous case for his retirement with enough passion that you almost believe it — then Larry's single question exposes the whole thing as theater. The joke is that Artie has already taken a job, mid-retirement speech. The structure (big passionate speech → one quiet question that destroys it) is very strong.

jokes.text: Artie on the Rosie O'Donnell show job: 'She wants to come back nice this time, so she wants to have me come around one day a week to scare the shit out of her staff.'
jokes.setup: Artie explains the Rosie job he's taken — it's just a consulting gig
jokes.punchline: His function at the Rosie show will be to 'scare the shit out of her staff' — implying Rosie O'Donnell's reputation for difficulty is best managed with someone more terrifying than her on staff
jokes.explanation: Artie's job description at Rosie — professional intimidation specialist — is perfect for his character and a sharp industry joke about what kind of person would be MORE feared than Rosie O'Donnell. 'Scare the shit out of her staff' as a job function is brilliantly specific and quotable. Strong Artie character integration.

jokes.text: Artie on the Roseanne job: 'Rosie wants to come back nice this time, so she wants to have me come around one day a week to scare the shit out of her staff.'
jokes.setup: Artie explains his 'consulting' role on Roseanne
jokes.punchline: His specific job description is to 'scare the shit out of her staff' — which is both a commentary on Roseanne's reputation and a perfect description of what Artie does naturally
jokes.explanation: The job description 'scare the shit out of her staff' is both a genuine industry joke (Roseanne's show was notorious for staff turnover and difficult behavior) and a perfect character moment — it's exactly what Artie would be hired for. The comedy of his 'retirement' being to scare people professionally is delicious. Justifies 8+ for originality of the conceit and for how it deepens Artie's character while being funny.

jokes.text: Hank returns sobbing — it's revealed he ran his car into the dumpster: 'I think I had the car in reverse and I ran into the fucking dumpster... and it hooked on my bumper.'
jokes.setup: Hank made a dramatic exit; now there's a loud crash and he returns crying
jokes.punchline: His operatic exit was ruined by a dumpster — his bumper is literally hooked to it. The sublime (grand emotional departure) meets the ridiculous (can't reverse out of a parking lot)
jokes.explanation: The perfect capstone to Hank's arc. He storms out with maximum dignity intact; the universe immediately strips it by hooking his car to a dumpster. The visual is inherently funny (a man crying, attached to a dumpster), and the detail — 'I think I had the car in reverse' — is delivered with such pitiful uncertainty that it compounds the comedy. Great structure: dignified exit → immediate humiliation → return to people he just cursed out for help.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Let's go to the Smokehouse and think this over.' Hank: 'I'm such a prick.'
jokes.setup: The three are heading out together after Hank's dramatic tantrum and dumpster incident
jokes.punchline: Hank's final line of the series is 'I'm such a prick' — the most self-aware thing he's ever said, delivered as they all walk out together
jokes.explanation: Four words to end a character's run on a show. 'I'm such a prick' is Hank's most complete moment of self-awareness and his funniest, simultaneously. It's funny because it's true and because he says it so casually, as if confirming a weather report. The economy is near-perfect. It's also the right ending: after all his rage and pathos, Hank reduces himself to this one honest line. Exceptional character integration — only Hank ends his story this way.

tmdb_overview: Part 2 of the final ever show. Larry is in hot water with Carol Burnet when he tells her she was the first person he chose to be on his final show. This doesn't appear to be the case as Ellen confirms. Bruno Kirby is bumped again. Clint Black sings goodbye to Larry.
